claims.text: The proposed starting material is a powder-metallurgy tungsten-based refractory or high-entropy alloy with a BCC matrix and few or no coherent nanoprecipitates.
Elemental powder mixing followed by rapid consolidation such as spark plasma sintering can produce in-situ TiC precipitates.
The processing intervention can produce a uniform TiC dispersion both inside grains and along grain boundaries.
The TiC precipitates produced by the intervention are nanoscale and coherent with the matrix.
TiC can be uniformly distributed within tungsten grains and along tungsten grain boundaries.
Coherent TiC interfaces act as dislocation bridges.
Coherent TiC interfaces facilitate dislocation transmission through the alloy microstructure.
The TiC dispersion promotes multistage strain hardening.
Coherent TiC interfaces reduce local stress concentrations.
The reduction of stress concentrations delays premature crack initiation.
A controlled TiC dispersion increases plastic strain before failure at temperatures above about 1000 °C.
A controlled TiC dispersion increases work-hardening capacity under high-temperature loading.
A controlled TiC dispersion improves fracture toughness under high-temperature loading.
Dispersed TiC improves elevated-temperature properties relevant to plasma-facing tungsten materials.
The proposed mechanism applies to refractory alloys having either a BCC or high-entropy matrix.
The proposed mechanism should hold above approximately 1000 °C.
The mechanism may not apply at lower temperatures.
Matrix-precipitate coherency is necessary for the proposed mechanism.
Comparing samples while holding grain size and phase composition constant would isolate the effect of TiC precipitation.
The magnitude of the improvements and the optimal TiC size and distribution remain unknown.

contradictions.description: The modified material is produced by adding or forming TiC, yet the baseline and experimental design require the TiC-containing and TiC-free alloys to have identical composition. Their overall compositions cannot be identical unless 'composition' is explicitly restricted to the matrix composition.

The intervention introduces a TiC phase, while the conditions require phase composition to remain constant between samples. TiC phase fraction or phase inventory must necessarily differ for the proposed comparison.
